launch_app.description: Launch an installed app by its store app id via the REST API. Reportedly unauthenticated on the Tizen fleet samsungtvws targets; treat a failure as "needs pairing" only after ruling out a wrong id — the REST surface predates the token model and does not consult it.

app_id.description: Samsung store app id, e.g. "3201606009684" or the well-known "org.tizen.browser" (launching it NATIVE_LAUNCH-style with a URL needs the WebSocket ed.apps.launch, not this endpoint). Opaque string; numeric-looking today.

press_back.description: Return one level (the physical Return key).

press_enter.description: D-pad centre — select the focused item.

press_fast_forward.description: Fast-forward; press repeatedly for faster speeds.

press_info.description: Info banner for the current programme/context.

press_power.description: Toggle power — in practice, the network power-OFF. 2016+ sets collapsed KEY_POWERON/KEY_POWEROFF into this one key.

press_previous_channel.description: Jump back to the previously watched channel.

press_rewind.description: Rewind; press repeatedly for faster speeds.

parse_rules: The description is ordinary UPnP device XML; the Samsung-specific deviceType urn:samsung.com:device:RemoteControlReceiver:1 is itself the confirmation this is a controllable Samsung TV.
friendlyName is user-set and typically looks like '[TV] Samsung Q60 Series (55)'; treat it as display text only.
The LOCATION port is the UPnP description port (commonly 9197 or 8001 depending on generation), NOT the control port — control is always 8001/8002 on the same host.
The same M-SEARCH may also answer urn:schemas-upnp-org:service:RenderingControl:1 with manufacturer 'Samsung Electronics' (Home Assistant matches this as a weaker third target); dedupe on UDN.

device.name: Samsung Tizen Smart TV (2016+)
device.notes: Samsung Smart TVs from 2016 onward run Tizen and expose a local control API on ports 8001 (plain) and 8002 (TLS). The control channel is a WebSocket to /api/v2/channels/samsung.remote.control; the first connection from an unknown client name pops an Allow/Deny dialog on the TV, and an approved connection is issued a reusable token in the ms.channel.connect event. Remote keys are injected as ms.remote.control JSON messages; apps are listed and launched with ms.channel.emit (ed.installedApp.get / ed.apps.launch) and a small unauthenticated REST API under /api/v2/ covers device info and app status/run/close/install. Discovery is SSDP (urn:samsung.com:device:RemoteControlReceiver:1). Pre-2016 Samsung Smart TVs (Orsay platform) speak a different protocol on TCP 55000 — see samsung_legacy_common.

openness.notes: Samsung has never published the local remote-control protocol; the developer site documents the (cloud-paired) Smart View SDK and web-app APIs, not the port-8001/8002 channel. Everything here is the consensus of the open-source clients that drive these TVs daily: samsungtvws (xchwarze/samsung-tv-ws-api, the library Home Assistant's samsungtv integration uses), samsungctl, and homebridge-samsung-tizen. Status is therefore "undocumented" even though the protocol is unusually well trodden for a closed one — the write-up below is a reconstruction from client source, not a summary of vendor text.

upstream_docs.covers: Which model families map to which year and Tizen version, i.e. which TVs are Tizen (2016+) and fall under this spec at all. Samsung publishes nothing about the local wire protocol itself.
upstream_docs.title: Samsung — TV model groups (model year ↔ Tizen version)

issued_to_client: WebSocket auth token, returned in the ms.channel.connect event after the user approves the first connection; reused as the token query parameter on port 8002.
credentials.notes: Access control is the approval prompt plus the token, not a password: any host on the same subnet can ASK to control the TV, but only approved client names get a working channel. Two settings shape this: General > External Device Manager > Device Connection Manager > Access Notification (default on newer TVs prompts on EVERY connection; "First Time Only" is what makes a stored token useful) and the Device List in the same menu, which revokes previously approved clients. Samsung TVs refuse WebSocket connections from a different subnet/VLAN — documented by both samsungtvws and Home Assistant — so network reachability is part of the security model whether the owner wants it or not.
stored_on_device: Device Connection Manager approved-client list (paired remote-control clients and their tokens)

factory_reset.effect: Clears network credentials, accounts, installed apps, picture/sound settings and the Device Connection Manager approved-client list; the TV returns to first-run setup. Every paired remote-control token dies with it.

steps.action: Settings > General > Reset (menu path varies slightly by year: on some models Settings > Support > Self Diagnosis > Reset).
Enter the security PIN (default 0000) and confirm; the TV reboots into first-run setup.

methods.description: First-run setup on the TV itself: language, network, passphrase via the on-screen keyboard, optional Samsung account sign-in. The account gates app-store installs, not local control.

steps.action: Power on the TV and follow the on-screen setup with the bundled remote.
Select the WiFi network (or plug in Ethernet) and enter the passphrase on the TV itself.
Discover the TV on the LAN.
steps.expect: A response whose LOCATION fetches a description with the Samsung RemoteControlReceiver deviceType.

steps.action: Confirm the REST API is reachable.
steps.expect: JSON device document (name, modelName, duid, network info) on port 8001.

steps.action: Open the WebSocket control channel; the TV shows an Allow/Deny prompt for the new client name — choose Allow.
steps.expect: Client receives ms.channel.connect with data.token; denial or timeout arrives as ms.channel.unauthorized.
steps.notes: The wire detail of this step is samsung_remote_common.pairing; it is a WebSocket, which the request vocabulary here cannot spell.

steps.action: Store the issued token and pass it as the token query parameter on every subsequent connection.

setup.notes: Onboarding happens on the TV's own screen (network selection, passphrase on the on-screen keyboard); there is no app-driven provisioning protocol to reimplement. What a LAN client must do instead is PAIR: the first WebSocket connection from a new client name raises an Allow/Deny dialog on the TV, and approval returns a reusable token in the ms.channel.connect event (samsung_remote_common.pairing). Medium confidence throughout: every step is what the open-source clients and Home Assistant's docs describe, replayed against no hardware here.

rejoin.notes: Settings > General > Network > Network Settings re-runs only the network step; a factory reset is never needed just to change routers.

entities.name: Power
entities.notes: Off only. KEY_POWER is nominally a toggle, but the network stack is down in standby, so no network client can reach an off set — from the network the key is discrete-off in practice, which is why this binds turn_off rather than toggle: the toggle direction is unreachable by construction (samsung_remote_common.power). Power-on is Wake-on-LAN, which this file has no vocabulary for, and no power state is readable. Render as a one-way off.

entities.name: Power Key
entities.notes: The raw remote key, distinct from the Power switch above: it promises a keypress, not a direction. Network power-off only; power-on is Wake-on-LAN (samsung_remote_common.power).

entities.name: Back
entities.notes: The physical Return key; KEY_RETURN on the wire.

entities.name: OK
entities.notes: D-pad centre; KEY_ENTER on the wire, and the trailing key of direct channel entry.

entities.name: Pause
entities.notes: Separate from Play on Samsung — there is no combined play/pause toggle key.

entities.name: Source
entities.notes: Opens the source list; specific inputs are then driven with the d-pad keys. There is no direct HDMI-n key on Tizen.

entities.name: HDMI
entities.notes: Cycles HDMI inputs on sets that map KEY_HDMI; model-dependent.

http_endpoints.description: JSON identity document: display name, modelName, model code, networkType, ip, wifiMac, duid, udn, resolution, Tizen-related versions (samsung_remote_common.app_control.device_info_example). The duid/wifiMac pair is the stable identity — and the WoL target — that the SSDP description lacks.
http_endpoints.name: Device Info

http_endpoints.description: Whether the named app is installed/running: {"id": ..., "name": ..., "running": true|false, "visible": ..., "version": ...}. App ids are the store's (e.g. "3201606009684", "org.tizen.browser"); there is no REST list, ids come from the WebSocket ed.installedApp.get event.
http_endpoints.name: App Status

http_endpoints.description: Launch (or foreground) an installed app by id. Empty body. The sendable half of Samsung app control — the WebSocket ed.apps.launch equivalent, and the only Tizen command in this file the reference app can execute today.
http_endpoints.name: Launch App

http_endpoints.description: Terminate a running app by id. Catalogued for completeness; the reference app's GET/POST-only command vocabulary cannot send it.
http_endpoints.name: Close App

http_endpoints.description: Install an app from the Samsung store by id. Same cataloguing caveat as Close App.
http_endpoints.name: Install App

samsung_legacy_common.applies_to: Pre-2016 Samsung Smart TVs on the Orsay platform (roughly 2011-2015: C/D/E/F series and most H/J series). Between the two sits a third, messier generation: H-series (2014) and part of J-series (2015) speak a WebSocket API on port 8001 wrapped in an AES-encrypted pairing exchange (the "encrypted" extra of samsungtvws, py3rijndael-based). That variant is noted here for completeness but NOT specified — treat it as an open research item, not as covered by either block in this file.
samsung_legacy_common.key_vocabulary: Same KEY_* names as the Tizen vocabulary (they share the remote), per samsungctl's table. The generational traps run the other way here: KEY_POWERON/KEY_POWEROFF exist on these sets where 2016+ collapsed them to KEY_POWER.
samsung_legacy_common.pairing: Same model as Tizen, older suit: the first connection from an unknown controller name raises the on-screen prompt, and approval is remembered per name/MAC. There is no token — the client simply reconnects.
samsung_legacy_common.responses: The TV answers with a 3-byte header whose bytes 1-2 are the little-endian length of a TV-name string, then the name, then a 2-byte little-endian length and the response body. Body 0x64 0x00 0x01 0x00 = access granted; 0x64 0x00 0x00 0x00 = denied; a body starting 0x0A = the TV is showing the Allow/Deny prompt (wait and read again); 0x65 = user cancelled; 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 = key accepted. An empty read means the TV hung up.
samsung_legacy_common.transport_gap: Raw TCP with a custom binary-ish envelope — also not one of the reference app's "http"/"soap" transports. Documented so the gap is recorded, not hidden.
samsung_legacy_common.wire_format: Every packet is a 3-byte header followed by a length-prefixed, base64-carrying payload. serialize(s) = [len(s) as one byte][0x00][s]; strings are base64-encoded BEFORE serializing. The handshake (sent once, on connect) is: outer header 0x00 0x00 0x00, then serialize-raw of an inner payload 0x64 0x00 + serialize(base64(description)) + serialize(base64(id)) + serialize(base64(name)) — the "controller string": a description/app-string, a client id, and the client name the TV's prompt will show (samsungctl defaults: description "PC", id "", name "samsungctl"; other clients famously use "iphone..iapp.samsung"). A key press is: outer header 0x00 0x00 0x00 + serialize-raw of inner payload 0x00 0x00 0x00 + serialize(base64("KEY_*")).

app_control.device_info_example: GET http://<ip>:8001/api/v2/ answers JSON shaped like {"id":"uuid:...","name":"[TV] Samsung 6 Series (55)","version":"2.0.25", "device":{"type":"Samsung SmartTV","duid":"...","model":"16_JAZZM_UHD", "modelName":"UE55KU6079","networkType":"wireless","ip":"...", "wifiMac":"...","udn":"uuid:...","resolution":"3840x2160",...}, "type":"Samsung SmartTV","uri":"http://<ip>:8001/api/v2/"}. device.duid / device.wifiMac are the stable identities the SSDP description does not carry; device.wifiMac is also what Wake-on-LAN needs.
app_control.over_rest: The same launches and lifecycle operations exist as plain unauthenticated REST (samsungtvws rest.py): GET/POST/DELETE/PUT /api/v2/applications/{appId} = status/run/close/install, and GET /api/v2/ = the device-info document. These are the endpoints in http_endpoints below. There is no REST app LIST; the list is the WebSocket ed.installedApp.get above, which is why no app-picker select entity exists here — options_source's contract is XML-over-HTTP and this list is JSON-over-WebSocket.
app_control.over_websocket: ms.channel.emit frames, params {"event": ..., "to": "host"}. ed.installedApp.get asks for the installed-app list, answered by an ed.installedApp event whose data is a JSON string of app records (appId, name, ...) — NOT answered on all models (samsungtvws waits up to 10s and gives up; see its issue #23). ed.apps.launch launches: params data {"action_type": "DEEP_LINK"|"NATIVE_LAUNCH", "appId": ..., "metaTag": ...}; opening a URL is org.tizen.browser with NATIVE_LAUNCH and the URL as metaTag.

connection.handshake: The TV speaks first. A good connection delivers an ms.channel.connect event whose data carries the new-or-reused token and the currently connected client list; the client must read and store data.token before sending anything. Refusal is an ms.channel.unauthorized event (user pressed Deny, or the prompt timed out) — surface it as "approve the connection on the TV", not as a network failure. Startup may also deliver client connect/disconnect noise events; samsungtvws ignores everything until it sees connect or unauthorized.
connection.subnet_rule: The TV refuses WebSocket connections that arrive from a different subnet/VLAN (both samsungtvws and the Home Assistant docs state this plainly). A client that can reach the REST API but never completes the WS handshake should suspect routing, not auth.
connection.url: <scheme>://<ip>:<port>/api/v2/channels/samsung.remote.control?name=<name>[&token=<token>] where scheme/port is ws/8001 or wss/8002, <name> is the client display name STANDARD-base64-encoded (samsungtvws: base64 of the UTF-8 name, e.g. 'SamsungTvRemote' -> 'U2Ftc3VuZ1R2UmVtb3Rl'), and token is the stored auth token (8002 only, when known).

key_injection.description: One JSON text frame per key event, method ms.remote.control. Cmd is Click (press+release, the normal case), Press, or Release — a held key is Press, a pause, then Release. DataOfCmd is the key name from the KEY_* vocabulary. Option is the literal string "false" and TypeOfRemote the literal "SendRemoteKey" for every key. Clients throttle repeats (samsungtvws defaults to a 1s key_press_delay).
key_injection.key_vocabulary: The commands block below names the common subset; the full published list (power, navigation, digits, channel, volume, inputs, media, colour keys, teletext, PIP, KEY_EXT1-41 and friends) is in samsungtvws COMMANDS.md and homebridge-samsung-tizen's command page — both self-described as unofficial, and individual keys vary by model and year. Known generational trap: pre-2016 KEY_POWEROFF/KEY_POWERON collapse to a single KEY_POWER toggle on 2016+ sets (Home Assistant key-table note).
key_injection.text_entry: Free text into a focused input field is TypeOfRemote "SendInputString" with DataOfCmd "base64" and Cmd the base64-encoded text, followed by a SendInputEnd message; some TVs additionally require a one-time ms.channel.emit broadcast of event "custom.remote.textReceived" before the first string (samsungtvws send_text). A cursor device exists too (TypeOfRemote "ProcessMouseDevice", Cmd "Move" with a Position object).

pairing.flow: No PIN, no shared secret: authorization is the user pressing Allow on the TV. First connection from an unknown name -> Allow/Deny dialog. Allow -> ms.channel.connect carries data.token; the client stores it and sends it as &token= on every later connection (8002). Deny or timeout -> ms.channel.unauthorized. The whole flow is driven by the client NAME in the URL, so a client that renames itself is a new stranger to the TV.
pairing.tv_settings: General > External Device Manager > Device Connection Manager: Access Notification set to "First Time Only" stops the prompt-every-time behaviour newer TVs default to (Home Assistant and samsungtvws both document this), and Device List is where stale approvals are revoked. Menu labels vary slightly by Tizen generation.

ports.8001: ws:// plain WebSocket + http:// REST under /api/v2/. Older Tizen sets (2016-2018 era) commonly listen here; per samsungtvws connection.py the token query parameter is only appended on the TLS port, so 8001 clients typically authenticate by client name alone.
ports.8002: wss:// WebSocket + https:// REST. TLS with the TV's self-signed certificate — clients disable verification (samsungtvws passes CERT_NONE). Newer Tizen sets listen here only; the token query parameter is appended when one is stored.

power.description: KEY_POWER turns the TV OFF from any network client, but no network command can turn a standby TV on — the network stack is down. Power-on is Wake-on-LAN to the MAC from device.wifiMac (Home Assistant does exactly this; it requires WoL enabled on the TV, and ethernet-connected sets wake more reliably than WiFi ones).

samsung_remote_common.transport_gap: NOT SUPPORTED by the reference app today: the app's command transports are "http" and "soap", and this channel is a persistent WebSocket with a token-auth handshake. A client must implement: RFC 6455 (including TLS with a self-signed cert on 8002), the ms.channel.connect / ms.channel.unauthorized handshake events, token capture and reuse, and keepalive for the session. The commands block below therefore declares the key commands with NO `transport` key — they inherit device.transport "websocket", and a consumer that only speaks http/soap must treat them as documented-but-not-sendable rather than rendering a dead control. Only launch_app (REST POST) is directly sendable today.

channels.description: The single control socket. Key presses, app launches and text entry all ride it.
channels.name: remote

pairing.prompt_notes: No PIN and no shared secret: authorisation is the viewer pressing Allow on the TV. A first connection under an unknown client name raises an Allow/Deny dialog; Allow delivers ms.channel.connect carrying data.token, which the client stores and sends as &token= on every later connection. Deny or a timeout delivers ms.channel.unauthorized — say "approve the connection on the TV", never "the network failed". The whole flow keys on the client NAME in the URL, so a client that renames itself is a new stranger and prompts again.
